parole.significato: A suffix forming infinitives of first conjugation verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āre, the ending of the present active infinitive form of first conjugation verbs. Cognate with Spanish -ar, French -er, Italian -are, etc.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the masculine singular past participle of regular -a (first conjugation) verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātus, from Proto-Italic *-ātos.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form the first-person singular and third-person plural present of most regular -i (fourth conjugati…
parole.testo: A form of the infix -esc-, from Latin -ēscō (and -ēscunt in the case of the third-person plural). Cognates include Aromanian -escu, Italian -isco, -iscono, Spanish -ezco, -ecen, Catalan -eixo, -eixen.
Inherited from Latin agrum (“field, ground”), itself from Proto-Italic *agros, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros.

parole.significato: fast, fasting (abstaining from or eating very little food)
parole.testo: Probably from Latin iēiūnium or iēiūnus through a Vulgar Latin root *iaiūnus > *aiūnus, from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”). Compare Spanish ayuno, French jeun, jeûne, also Italian digiuno. The equivalent Aromani
Inherited from Latin albus, from Proto-Italic *alβos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élbʰos, *álbʰos, *albʰós (“white”). Doublet of album.
From Latin annus (“year”), from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”). Compare Megleno-Romanian an and Aromanian an.
Inherited from Latin arāre, from Proto-Italic *araō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éryeti (“to plough”), from the root *h₂erh₃-.
Inherited from Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom.
Borrowed from Latin (mensis) augustus. Compare also the inherited doublets agust and gust.
Inherited from Latin aurum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- (“glow”), from *h₂ews- (“to dawn, become light, become red”).
Inherited from Latin habēre (“have, hold, possess”), probably from a Proto-Italic *haβēō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰh₁bʰ- (“to grab, to take”).
Inherited from Latin barba, Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”). Compare Aromanian barbã.
Inherited from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti.

Inherited from Latin vōcem, accusative singular of vōx, from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs. Boace was largely supplanted by the Slavicism glas, which was itself later replaced by the borrowed doublet voce during the period of Re-Latinisation of Romanian. Cognate to Aromanian bo
Inherited from Latin bonus, from Old Latin duenos, later duonus, from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Doublet of bon, bonă, and bonus.
Inherited from Latin carnem, accusative of carō, from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”). Compare Aromanian carni, carne.
Inherited from Latin cernere, from Proto-Italic *krinō, from Proto-Indo-European *krey-.
Inherited from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kert(e)snā, from Proto-Indo-European *kert-sna, from *ker-, *sker-.
Inherited from Latin crēscere, from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).
Inherited from Latin cum, from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”). Cognate with Sicilian cu.
Inherited from Latin culmen, from Proto-Italic *kolamen, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH-.
Probably derived from Latin cōlāre (“to filter, strain”) as well as Latin currere, from Proto-Italic *korzō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers-. Mostly replaced by the modified variant form curge.

Inherited from Latin currere (“run, flow”), an alteration of the older / regional form cure, influenced by verbs like merge. Likewise in most areas where cure is the dominant pronunciation, merge is altered to mere - by the same analogy. See also scurge. The Latin is from Proto-Italic *korzō, itself

Inherited from Latin cacāre, from Proto-Italic *kak(k)āō, from Proto-Indo-European *kakka- (imitative root related to defecation). Compare Italian cagare, French chier, Spanish cagar, Portuguese cagar.

parole.significato: a sheep with long and straight wool
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin caprina, feminine of caprinus.
Inherited from Latin catīnum, from catīnus, from Proto-Italic *katinos.
From Latin dare, ultimately from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”). Compare Aromanian dau, dari, Italian dare, Spanish dar.
Inherited from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁.
Inherited from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.
Inherited from Latin dūcere, from Proto-Italic *doukō, from Proto-Indo-European *déwketi, from the root *dewk-. Reinforcement by Italian ducere is possible.
Inherited from Latin dolēre, from Proto-Italic *doleō (“hurt, cause pain”), from Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁éyeti (“divide”), from *delh₁- (“cut”).
Inherited from Latin fāgus, from Proto-Italic *fāgos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“beech tree”).
Inherited from Latin flōrem, accusative of flōs, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”). Doublet of floră.
Borrowed from Latin forum.
Inherited from Latin fūmus, from Proto-Italic *fūmos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós.
Inherited from Latin fūr, from Proto-Italic *fōr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰṓr, from the root *bʰer- (“to carry”).

Inherited from Latin gentem most likely through a Vulgar Latin *gentum or *gentus (see împărat for a similar evolution). Doublet of gintă, which was borrowed. Compare Aromanian ghimtã, Dalmatian ziant.
Inherited from Latin gustus, from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.
Inherited from Latin jugum, iugum, from Proto-Italic *jugom, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.
Inherited from Latin lēgem, accusative of lēx, from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s, from *leǵ- (“to gather”).
Inherited from Latin locus.
Inherited from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-. Compare Aromanian lunã.
Inherited from Latin lupus, from an Osco-Umbrian language, from Proto-Italic *lukʷos, metathesis of Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos. Doublet of lupus.
From Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.
Inherited from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.
Inherited from Latin mīca, from Proto-Italic *smīkā, from Proto-Indo-European *smeyg- (“small, thin, delicate”).
Inherited from Latin mīlia, plural of mīlle, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”). Doublet of milă. Compare Albanian mijë.
Inherited from Latin medius, from Proto-Italic *meðios, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare mediu, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Latin mentem, accusative singular of mēns, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”). Compare Aromanian minti.

Inherited from Latin nātus, from earlier gnātus, from Proto-Italic *gnātos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁tós (“begotten, produced”), derived from the root *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, give birth”). The meaning in Romanian developed from that of "offspring" or "progeny" in relation to the parent. Compare Ar
Inherited from Latin nivem, accusative singular of nix (“snow”), from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs.
Inherited from Latin nepōs, nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Compare Italian nipote, French neveu, Catalan nebot, Aromanian nipot.
Inherited from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Compare Aromanian noapti.
Inherited from Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs. Compare Aromanian noi.
Inherited from Latin noster, nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.
Inherited from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos.
Inherited from Latin ovem, accusative of ovis, from Proto-Italic *owis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis (“sheep”) or *h₃éwis. Compare Aromanian oai.
Inherited from Latin olla, from Proto-Italic *aukslā, from Proto-Indo-European *Hukʷsleh₂, Proto-Indo-European *Hukʷ- (“cooking pot”).

Inherited from Latin hospitem, accusative singular of hospes, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European noun *gʰóstipotis (whence also gospodin), a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. See also oaste. Compare Aromanian
Inherited from Latin hostem, accusative singular of hostis (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“guest, stranger”).

Inherited from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan os, French os, Italian osso, Portuguese osso, Sardinian ossu, Spanish hueso.
From the older form peană, from Latin pinna, penna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).
Inherited from Latin pālus (“stake”), from Proto-Italic *pākslos, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-slos, from *peh₂ǵ-.
Inherited from Latin partem, accusative of pars, from Proto-Italic *partim. Compare Aromanian parti.

parole.significato: father (term of address for a Christian priest)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pater.
Inherited from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Compare Sardinian batero, batoro, batro, baturu.
Inherited from Latin pāscere from Proto-Italic *pāskō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect”). Compare Aromanian pascu.

Inherited from Latin pectus, from Proto-Italic *pektos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peg- (“breast”). Compare Catalan pit, Italian petto, Portuguese peito, Spanish pecho, Aromanian cheptu, chiept, chept.
Inherited from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Cognates at the Latin entry. . Doublet of plen.
Inherited from Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Doublet of the borrowed plantă.
Inherited from Latin porca.
Inherited from Latin pōmus, from Proto-Italic *poomos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”), from *h₂epo (“off”) + *h₁em- (“take”). See pōmum.

parole.significato: pig (mammal of genus Sus), hog, swine
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”).
Inherited from Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, *puḱnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).
Inherited from Latin pōnere, from Proto-Italic *posnō.
Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

Inherited from Latin rubus (“bramble, briar”), from Proto-Italic *wruðos, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰo- (“sweetbriar”). Compare Italian rovo, dialectal rogo. For the sound shift of Latin -b- to -g- in Romanian, compare neg, negură.
Inherited from Latin rīpa, from Proto-Italic *reipā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁réyp-eh₂ (“steep slope”), from *h₁reyp- (“to tear, tear down”).
Inherited from Latin scrībere, from Proto-Italic *skreiβō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kreybʰ-.

From soarte (now considered archaic), from Latin sortem, accusative of sors (“fate”), from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). An alternative theory derives it from Latin exorta, from exortus (“appeared”), but is less likely.
Inherited from Latin spīnus, from spīna, from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”). Compare Aromanian schin.
With apocope from colloquial steauă, from archaic steală, from Latin stēlla, from Proto-Italic *stērolā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. Doublet of aster and star.
Inherited from Latin tendere, from Proto-Italic *tendō, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).
Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Aromanian trei.
From Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.
Inherited from Latin tacēre, from Proto-Italic *takēō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tak- or *tHk-.
Inherited from Latin tuus, probably through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *tous or *teus. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *towos.

Inherited from Latin ūber, from Proto-Italic *ouðer, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”). The change of the Latin consonant -b- to Romanian -g- is also witnessed in rug, neg, etc. In this case, it may also have been influenced by suge (“to suck”). The regional variant may have been influen
Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Latin ungere, from earlier unguō, from Proto-Italic *ongʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”). Compare Aromanian ungu.

Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one, single”). The reason why unu was exempt from the widespread dropping of word-final /u/ at the time was because the word’s use is reserved for counting only, whereas its doub
Inherited from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos.
Inherited from Latin vadum (“shallow, ford”), from Proto-Italic *waðom, from Proto-Indo-European *wh₂dʰóm, from *weh₂dʰ-.
Inherited from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Compare Aromanian ved, videari, Italian vedere.
Inherited from Latin venīre, from Proto-Italic *gʷenjō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷm̥yéti, from zero-grade of *gʷem- + *-yéti.

parole.significato: to have life; to live, exist
parole.testo: From an older form vie, from Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).
Inherited from Latin vermis, vermem, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.
Inherited from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.

Generally taken as inherited from Latin vīta (“life”), from Proto-Italic *gʷītā. In this view, the shift toward the meaning “animal” is sometimes explained as Slavic influence; compare Bulgarian животно (životno, “animal”) alongside живот (život, “life”). Another possibility is a back-formation from
Inherited from Latin vīvus, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós.
Inherited from Latin vōs, from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs.
Inherited from Latin voster, vostrum, from vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.
Inherited from Latin vulpēs, vulpem, from earlier volpēs, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl(o)p- ~ *h₂ulp- (“(red) fox”).
Inherited from Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts < *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
Inherited from Latin deus, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós. Doublet of zău.
Inherited from Latin dīcere, present active participle of dīcō, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).
Inherited from Latin in. Cognate with English in.
From an older form șea, from Latin sella, from Proto-Italic *sedlā, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-. See also șale.
Inherited from Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.

Inherited from Latin servus, from Proto-Italic *serwos (“guardian”), from Proto-Indo-European *serwos (“guardian”), possibly from *ser- (“watch over, protect”). Doublet of serv, which was a borrowing.
From the original form ținea (a second-conjugation verb), from Latin tenēre, from Proto-Italic *tenēō, stative from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).
